newsitem.title: USA: Town mourns 10 killed in N.C. crash.
newsitem.headline: Town mourns 10 killed in N.C. crash.

text.p: A small town mourned the loss of 10 teenagers, and family members visited the wreck site Thursday where a tractor-trailer and a van carrying members of a high school marching band collided.

The collision Wednesday was the worst in recent state history. It occurred outside Plymouth in rural Washington County about 100 miles east of Raleigh as the students were returning from lunch to a marching band camp.
Thursday Myrtle Gordon stood atop an embankment and stared into the ravine where the van, carrying Plymouth High School students, came to rest.
"She was my only girl," Gordon said of Felicia Davis, 15, her voice barely audible. "She had her life planned."

The crumpled van had been removed but reminders of the collision remained. The smell of spilled fuel hung in the air and skid marks were visible on the pavement and grass. A heart-shaped memorial of flowers was placed on a wire stand, with a baseball cap attached to it and a clarinet reed beneath.
"She was going to finish school here, then go to Philadelphia to study to be a lawyer," Gordon said of Davis.

Plymouth's 4,000 residents were in mourning as well. Signs of sympathy were placed in many business windows, including one made by Mitchell Nowarah, owner of Washington County Seafood: "God bless the victims of the Highway 45 accident."

At Plymouth High, floral arrangements from neighbouring schools and businesses filled the office. Classmates remembered the dead as bright, fun-loving and dedicated. Classes resume Aug. 18 after the summer vacation.

"It's going to hit hard when we get out on the field and see all those empty spaces, but we're going to be strong," student Terrance James, 15, of the school's marching band, said. "No goofing off. We're dedicating it to the friends we lost."
Local media reported that the van's driver, Damien Burden, 17, had tried to pass three vehicles in a no-passing zone. But Highway Patrol officials said the investigation was incomplete.
James said Burden was a conscientious driver who did not take chances.
"If he was passing, he made sure he had plenty of room," James said. "He missed something. I just don't think he saw that third car."
